890.title: Pascal's night of fire (1654)
890.hook: a mathematician has an experience one night and writes Fire, sewing the note into his coat
890.howItsDone: Pascal's note, often called the Memorial, is read by Christians of different churches as a witness to a personal encounter with God, and some keep a copy of it or a short line from scripture close by in a similar way.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a burden tumbling into the Sepulchre in Bunyan's dream. Your line was the burden rolled away.

After Blaise Pascal dies, a servant going through his clothes feels something stiff in the lining of his coat. Tucked inside, the story goes, is a folded piece of parchment, and inside that, a scrap of paper, both in Pascal's handwriting. He had sewn it in, and he is said to have moved it from coat to coat, never mentioning it to anyone. Pascal was a mathematician and inventor, a man of numbers and proofs. But the note isn't a proof. It's barely sentences. Near the top, one word.

The word is Fire. The note gives the hours: from about half past ten at night until about half past midnight. Pascal didn't try to explain what happened. He wrote in bursts, like someone catching his breath. Right after Fire, he writes, in effect: the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, the God of Jacob, not of the philosophers and scholars. That's striking from a man who was a philosopher and a scholar. He isn't throwing away his mind. He's saying what met him that night wasn't an idea he'd reasoned his way to. It was the God of a family story, who calls people by name. Those three names come straight from scripture. In Exodus, Moses sees a bush on fire that doesn't burn up. In the King James words, "the bush burned with fire, and the bush was not consumed." And the voice from the fire says, "I am the God of thy father, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob." Pascal's night echoes that scene: a fire, and a God known by the people he has met. Further down, Pascal reaches for more words: certainty, feeling, joy, peace. Joy, again and again, and tears of joy. Then he sews it into his coat, not to show anyone, but to keep it close. Some readers see the note as the hidden center of everything he wrote afterward. Nobody can say exactly what he saw. He gave us one word for it, and kept it against his chest.

Think of a moment you've never quite been able to explain: a moment of awe, of love, of being met, of clarity. Don't tell yourself the whole story; let it come back in the quiet, and wait for one word to rise for it, the way Pascal had Fire. If you pray, hold that moment before God; if you don't, simply hold it and let the word arrive.
Pascal. The mathematician who had a night of fire, writing one word for what he felt and keeping it sewn into his coat.
Your line: fire. One word for a whole night, kept close. Day eight hundred ninety, done.

891.title: The Pietists
891.hook: Spener and the Pietists gather small groups to read the Bible and live it warmly
891.howItsDone: Christians in different churches meet in small groups, often in homes, to read a passage of the Bible together, talk about how to live it, and pray for one another.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Pascal's night of fire, one word sewn into a coat. Your line was fire.

What happens to a sermon after the last hymn? People shake hands at the door, go home, eat lunch. By Tuesday, it's mostly gone. A Lutheran pastor in Frankfurt named Philipp Jakob Spener worried about exactly that. His church had careful teaching, strong doctrine, faithful services. And yet faith, to him, seemed to stop at the church door. So he tried something small. He invited a few people to his house during the week to talk over the sermon and read the Bible together. Not a new church. Just a few chairs, an open book, and a question: how do we actually live this?

Spener wrote his hopes for the church in a short book called Pia Desideria, a Latin title usually rendered as pious longings, or heartfelt desires. Among them: that ordinary Christians would read the whole Bible, not just hear bits of it on Sunday. That every believer would take part in the church's life, not only the clergy, an echo of Luther's priesthood of all believers. That faith would show up in love, in how people actually treated each other. And that arguments about doctrine would be carried on with charity, not cruelty. The small groups that met in his home and others like them were sometimes called gatherings of piety. Critics called them Pietists, and in time the movement carried the name. Spener wasn't trying to throw out Lutheran teaching. He was trying to warm it. The Pietists spoke of a heart religion: faith you don't just agree to, but live. They found a model in the letter of James, in the King James words: "But be ye doers of the word, and not hearers only." And Jesus' promise in Matthew sets the size: "where two or three are gathered together in my name, there am I in the midst of them." The movement had its tensions; some church leaders worried small groups would split congregations, and the Pietists argued about that among themselves. But the idea traveled. A Bible study or house group today can look a lot like Spener's living room.

Bring to mind two or three people you could sit with, at a kitchen table or on a video call, to read something that matters and talk about living it. Hold their faces in the quiet. If you pray, pray for them by name or rest with where two or three are gathered; if you don't, simply hold the picture of that table.

892.title: The Moravians' hundred-year prayer
892.hook: at Herrnhut, a quarrelsome refugee village starts a prayer watch that tradition says ran for a century
892.howItsDone: Some Christian communities still keep a prayer watch the way Herrnhut did: people sign up for hours on a shared schedule so that someone is praying at every hour, day and night.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Pietists, small groups reading the Bible around a table. Your line was a heart religion.

On a nobleman's estate in Saxony, a village is going up fast. The newcomers are religious refugees, some from Moravia, joined by others with their own convictions and their own grudges. The estate belongs to a young count named Zinzendorf, shaped by the Pietists we met yesterday, and he's let them settle. They call the place Herrnhut. Almost at once, they're fighting: about doctrine, about leadership, about who's right. A refuge has turned into an argument. Zinzendorf goes house to house, talking, listening, pleading. Then something changes, and out of the change comes a prayer that, tradition says, didn't stop for a century.

The Moravian story remembers the turn this way. After months of quarrels, the community agrees on a shared way of living together, and then gathers for communion. Those present later described a deep sense of being made one, forgiven and reconciled, at the Lord's table. Soon after, a small group of men and women decide to keep a watch of prayer. Each person takes an hour, linked one into the next, so that at any time of day or night, someone in Herrnhut is praying. Tradition says the chain kept going for about a hundred years, passed from one generation to the next. Later tellings link the idea to an old command about the altar in Leviticus, in the King James words: "The fire shall ever be burning upon the altar; it shall never go out." In Hebrew, that's esh tamid, a fire that is always there. The Moravians weren't keeping a flame on stone. They were keeping prayer alive in people. Isaiah has a picture for it too: "I have set watchmen upon thy walls, O Jerusalem, which shall never hold their peace day nor night." No one person prayed for a hundred years, or through every night. Each took one hour, and trusted the others with the rest. The watch worked only because it was shared, and a quarreling village became a community that took turns holding the world before God. Out of that same community, missionaries soon went out across the seas, and some of them, as tomorrow's story shows, ended up on a ship in a storm.

Let these few minutes be one hour of the watch, in miniature. Breathe in, and bring to mind someone who needs to be held; breathe out, and keep them there, praying for them if you pray, or holding them in your attention if you don't.

893.title: The storm at sea
893.hook: crossing to Georgia, John Wesley is terrified; Moravian families sing calmly
893.howItsDone: Christians in different churches sing hymns and psalms in hard times, at bedsides, and at funerals, the way the Moravians sang through the storm.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Herrnhut and the Moravians' watch, one hour each, so the fire never went out. Your line was the watch of prayer.

A ship is crossing the Atlantic, bound for the colony of Georgia. On board is a young Church of England clergyman named John Wesley: serious, disciplined, on his way to be a missionary. He prays on a strict schedule. He fasts. He keeps a careful journal of how he spends his hours. And he is afraid of dying. Also on board are German Moravians, families from the movement we met yesterday, men, women and children. Wesley has been watching them: how humble they are, how willing to do the dirty jobs nobody else wants. Then the weather turns.

Wesley tells it in his journal. The Moravians are holding their evening service, in the middle of the opening psalm, when the sea breaks over the ship, splits the mainsail, and pours in between the decks. A terrible screaming starts among the English passengers. Then, in Wesley's plain sentence: "The Germans calmly sung on." Afterward, Wesley asks one of them if he wasn't afraid. The man answers, "I thank God, no." Weren't the women and children afraid? The man replies, mildly, "No; our women and children are not afraid to die." Wesley writes it all down. He's a clergyman and a missionary who has worked hard at his religion, and he has just watched these families face death with a calm he doesn't have. That gap troubles him, and sends him looking for whatever it is they know. The scene echoes a gospel story. In Mark, Jesus is asleep in a boat during a great storm, and the terrified disciples wake him. He speaks to the wind and the sea, "Peace, be still," and there's a great calm. Then he turns to them: "Why are ye so fearful? how is it that ye have no faith?" On Wesley's ship, the sea doesn't calm. The storm goes on. What's calm is the singing. The danger is real, and the Moravians are in it with everyone else. They sing in the middle of it, and a frightened young clergyman is paying attention, which is where tomorrow's story begins.

Bring to mind something that frightens you right now, small or large, and let it be there. Then let a steadying song come, a hymn, a psalm, a lullaby someone sang to you, and hum it or hear it in your head while the fear is still in the room. If you pray, let the song be your prayer, or rest with Jesus' words: peace, be still.
John Wesley. The frightened young clergyman who watched Moravian families keep singing while a storm broke over their ship to Georgia.
Your line: they were not afraid. They sang in the storm, not after it. Day eight hundred ninety-three, done.

894.title: Aldersgate (1738)
894.hook: at a quarter to nine, Wesley feels his heart strangely warmed
894.howItsDone: Some Methodist and Wesleyan churches mark Aldersgate Day by reading Wesley's journal entry aloud, and some Christians keep a habit of reviewing the day each evening to notice where God met them.

segments.voice: Yesterday, John Wesley in the storm, watching families sing as the waves broke. Your line was they were not afraid.

"In the evening I went very unwillingly to a society in Aldersgate Street." That's John Wesley, back in London after Georgia. The mission didn't go well. He's come home discouraged, still haunted by the calm he saw on that ship, still asking what those Moravian families knew. A society, in his world, is a small group meeting in a room to pray and read. He doesn't want to go. He goes anyway. Someone is reading aloud from an old book: Martin Luther's preface to Paul's letter to the Romans. Not a thrilling evening, on paper.

A little further on, in his own words: "About a quarter before nine, while he was describing the change which God works in the heart through faith in Christ, I felt my heart strangely warmed." He goes on: he felt he did trust in Christ, Christ alone, for salvation, and an assurance was given him that his sins were taken away, even his. Three things stand out. First, the time. Wesley, the man of schedules, notes it, about a quarter before nine, the way you'd remember where you were when the phone rang with news. Second, strangely. Not dramatic or loud: strange, unfamiliar, perhaps something he hadn't felt that way before, from a man who'd been doing religious things all his life. Third, warmed. Not blazing. Warmed. In Luke's gospel, two disciples walk to Emmaus with a stranger who explains the scriptures to them. Only later do they realize it was the risen Jesus, and they say to each other, "Did not our heart burn within us, while he talked with us by the way?" Wesley's evening has the same shape: words read aloud, and a heart that responds before the head has caught up. Methodists remember this evening, and Christians in other churches tell the story too. But hear what came before and after. Before, a man who had tried hard, gone unwillingly, and been honest about his fear. After, as his journal shows, he still had doubts and dry days. Aldersgate wasn't the end of the road. It was a turn in it.

Look back over the last week for a moment, maybe a small one, when something in you warmed: a sentence someone said, a song, a kindness, a line you read. Don't judge it as big or small; just find it and stay with it, where you were, roughly what time. If you pray, give thanks for it; if you don't, let yourself remember it fully.

895.title: Wesley on horseback
895.hook: a clergyman who loved order takes to the saddle and preaches in fields to working people
895.howItsDone: Methodist churches grew from Wesley's societies and classes, and Christians in different churches still take worship outdoors, to street corners, parks and workplaces, to meet people who don't come inside.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Aldersgate, and a heart strangely warmed. Your line was a quarter before nine.

John Wesley likes things done properly. He's a Church of England clergyman, trained at Oxford, and he believes preaching belongs in a church, from a pulpit, in good order. He later admits he'd been so attached to decency and order that saving souls outside a church would once have seemed to him almost a sin. But churches are closing their pulpits to him. To some clergy, his preaching is too warm, too urgent. Meanwhile, outside the city, there are working people, coal miners among them, who seldom if ever set foot in a parish church. So Wesley has a choice.

He goes outside. His journal records the day he first preached in the open air, and the phrase is startling: he "submitted to be more vile." He's borrowing from King David. In Second Samuel, as the ark of God comes into Jerusalem, David dances before the LORD with all his might, and his wife Michal despises him for it. David answers, "I will yet be more vile than thus." In other words: if worship makes me look undignified, so be it. So the man of order stands on a rise of ground in a field to preach. From then on, he travels. On horseback, year after year, along muddy roads and through all weathers, to towns, villages, mining districts, marketplaces. Tradition says he read books in the saddle, letting the horse find the way. When church officials objected that he was preaching in other men's parishes, he answered with a line from his journal: "I look upon all the world as my parish." Wherever he was, he felt bound to share the good news with anyone willing to hear. He didn't gather them into a new church at first. Wesley stayed a Church of England clergyman and urged his hearers to go to their parish churches. He organized them into small groups, societies and classes, to meet and pray between Sundays, and those groups became the Methodist movement. Jesus tells a parable about a feast where the invited guests won't come, so the host sends his servant out, in the King James words, "into the highways and hedges." Wesley took the road literally.

Bring to mind one person who won't come to you: a neighbor, a relative, a coworker, an old friend. Picture where they actually are today, their kitchen, their shift, their bench in the park, and hold them there as you breathe. If you pray, pray for them by name; if you don't, wonder what it would take to go to them instead of waiting.

Your line: the world is my parish. The road, as well as the pulpit. Day eight hundred ninety-five, done.

896.title: Charles Wesley's hymns
896.hook: John's brother writes hymns like O for a thousand tongues and Love divine, all loves excelling
896.howItsDone: Charles Wesley's hymns appear in the hymnbooks of different churches, and congregations sing them on Sundays and at Christmas, weddings and funerals, often standing together.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Wesley on horseback, and the Methodist movement taking shape in the fields. Your line was the world is my parish.

John Wesley rode the roads. His younger brother Charles rode them too, and did something else on the way: he wrote hymns. Lots of them. Tradition says he composed lines on horseback and, when one came, would stop at a house and ask for pen and ink before he lost it. If you've sung Hark! the herald angels sing in a church at Christmas, you've sung Charles Wesley. If you've been at a wedding where they sang Love divine, all loves excelling, you've sung him too. Both brothers preached, and Charles also set the message to music.

Here are the lines that open the hymn as it's usually sung today: "O for a thousand tongues to sing My great Redeemer's praise, The glories of my God and King, The triumphs of his grace!" The idea is simple and a little funny. One tongue isn't enough. Charles wants a thousand, because he can't say it all with one. Some readers hear in it the spirit of the Methodist revival: gratitude too big for a single voice. His hymns did a quiet job too. A hymn sung every week is carried in memory, whether or not the singer can read. People learned what the revival believed, about grace, about the cross, about a heart made new, by singing it until it was theirs. Another: "Love divine, all loves excelling, Joy of heaven, to earth come down." Love, here, is a name for God, and it comes down to earth; the hymn goes on to ask that love to make its home in the singer. His hymns fit an instruction in the letter to the Ephesians, where Christians are told to be filled with the Spirit, "Speaking to yourselves in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing and making melody in your heart to the Lord." Speaking to yourselves: a hymn isn't only sung up to God. It's sung across the room, to each other, and back into your own chest. And the last psalm has a line that fits too: "Let every thing that hath breath praise the LORD." A thousand tongues, every breath. Today his hymns are sung in churches of many kinds, far beyond the Methodists.

Say or sing today's first lines: O for a thousand tongues to sing my great Redeemer's praise. Then, since one tongue isn't enough, let the things you're grateful for come up one at a time, each with its own voice. If you pray, let that list be your praise; if you don't, let it grow.
Love divine. One of Charles Wesley's hymns, naming God's love that comes down to earth and asks to make its home in the singer.
Your line: o for a thousand tongues. One voice was never going to be enough. Sing on.
